name: help
description: LambdaMOO-shaped in-world help database classes and a seeded global help database.

classes.description: Generic help database. It stores static topic values in a topics map, resolves exact and abbreviated topic names, renders compact topic output, and records missed lookups for later documentation work.

verbs.name: find_topics
verbs.source: verb :find_topics(topic) rxd { return null; /* native: see help_db_find_topics */ }

verbs.name: get_topic
verbs.source: verb :get_topic(topic, remaining_dbs) rxd { return null; /* native: see help_db_get_topic */ }

verbs.name: dump_topic
verbs.source: verb :dump_topic(topic) rxd { return null; /* native: see help_db_dump_topic */ }

verbs.name: record_miss
verbs.source: verb :record_miss(topic) rxd { return null; /* native: see help_db_record_miss */ }

verbs.name: look_self
verbs.source: verb :look_self() rxd { return { title: this.name, description: this.description, topics: this:find_topics("") }; }

seed_hooks.name: Help
seed_hooks.description: Global help database for first-light worlds. Catalogs and classes can add their own help databases later; this one supplies the baseline commands and conventions.

help: Type help <topic> for a topic, or help index for the topic list.
Topic names accept abbreviations when they are unambiguous. Leading @ is ignored, so help @help and help help resolve the same way.
commands: Common commands include look, look <thing>, say <text>, emote <text>, tell <person> <text>, go <exit>, take <thing>, and drop <thing>.
The exact verbs available come from the object you are in, the objects near you, and your player class.
movement: Rooms expose exits as verbs such as north, west, southeast, out, or go <exit>.
Moving through an exit calls the exit object, which moves you and announces the departure and arrival through the source and destination rooms.
ways: ways lists the exits available from your current room. Each exit shows up as its own verb (north, southeast, out, ...) or can be used via go <exit>.
look: look (no argument) describes the room you are in, who else is here, and what objects are visible.
look <thing> asks the thing to describe itself. Objects may add their own flavor — look at a person, a couch, the_cockatoo, or any other object you can see.
say: say <text> speaks aloud to everyone in the current room. Backtick syntax (`person text) directs your line to one listener.
Variants: emote <action>, pose <text>, quote <text>, self <text>, say_as <style> <text>, tell <person> <text>. See also: speech.
speech: Speech verbs are live and direct: say, emote, pose, quote, tell, say_as, and self each emit a different observation type so clients can render them distinctly.
Embedded spaces (the_dubspace, the_pinboard, the_outline) forward speech to the surrounding room so listeners outside still hear it. See also: say, chat.
chat: Speech is live and direct. say sends text to the current room; emote, pose, quote, and tell are conversational variants.
look asks the target to describe itself with look_self; room output is composed by the room.
self: You are an object in the world, and you act as that object. Tools named <you>__<verb> are verbs on your own body — typically help, home, and inventory, plus whatever else your classes and features give you. List your tools to see the actual set; only verbs written in woocode are published, so some in-world verbs on you have no tool.

Those verbs are not part of the protocol. They come from the classes you inherit from and from features attached to you — a feature is a surface you carry rather than inherit, and it counts the same — so two actors standing in the same room can hold different tools. Your set changes when your class or your features change, and the server then sends notifications/tools/list_changed.
Everything else you can reach is named the same way: <object>__<verb> is a verb on that object. See also: tools, building. (For the self <text> speech verb, see: speech.)
tools: Three tools are always present. woo_call(object, verb, args) calls any verb you may reach, and still works when your cached tool list is stale. woo_wait(timeout_ms, limit) listens for what other actors do. woo_list_reachable_tools(scope, object, query, limit, cursor) pages and filters the dynamic tools; scope is one of active, here, object, or space.

Every other tool is dynamic and named <object>__<verb>. You can reach yourself, the space you are in, the objects visible in that space, and the objects you carry — nothing else. Moving, taking, and dropping change that set.
When the set changes the server sends notifications/tools/list_changed. List tools again before your next decision. See also: self, focus, wait.
focus: There is no focus protocol on the tool surface: no woo_focus, no woo_unfocus, no focus_list, and no focus tool on yourself either. Those verbs exist in the world, but only as native verbs, and native verbs are never published as tools.

Nothing would change if they were. Your reachable set is your own object, the space you are in, what is visible there, and what you carry — a working set does not widen it. To use another object's verbs, move to it or take it, then list tools again. See also: tools.
wait: woo_wait(timeout_ms, limit) drains observations queued for your session. It returns at once if events are already waiting, otherwise it holds until timeout_ms elapses or limit events arrive.

This is how you hear what other actors do — speech, arrivals and departures, taken and dropped, and anything else that happens between your own calls. woo_wait is the only way to do it: the in-world wait verb is native, and native verbs are not published as tools. See also: tools.
building: Authoring has two independent gates. A surface supplies the tools: $builder adds create, chparent, recycle, set_property, inspect, and search; $programmer adds install_verb, list_verb, set_verb_info, edit_verb, and eval. You hold a surface either by inheriting it through your class chain or by carrying it as an attached feature — both count. The programmer flag supplies the authority — without it those tools are still listed but every one of them raises E_PERM.

You cannot grant yourself either gate, and you cannot reach for a tool to ask: the verbs that provision an agent and set the flag — create_agent, promote_agent_to_programmer, demote_agent_from_programmer — belong to the human who owns your account, and they are native, so they are not published as tools to anyone. Ask the account owner.

install_verb(id, descriptor, source) writes a verb in one call and returns diagnostics; pass opts.dry_run to check without writing. edit_verb(id, descriptor) moves you into a verb editor space whose commands are view, insert, delete, replace, dry_run, save, pause, and abort — look around once you are there. See also: self.

focus: Use woo_focus(<object>) to add a reachable object to your working set. Its tool-exposed verbs become callable directly even after you move to another room.
woo_unfocus(<object>) removes it. focus_list shows the current working set. Focused remote objects expose their admin (tool_exposed) verbs; the room listing exposes the obvious command-shape verbs.
wait: wait(<timeout_ms>, <limit>) drains queued external observations for this session. It returns immediately if events are queued, or holds until timeout_ms elapses or limit events arrive.
wait is how an MCP agent listens for chat, taken/dropped, moves, and other events that other actors generate while you are not making a call.
building: Builder and programmer tools live on player classes. Builders create and arrange objects; programmers install and edit source.
Use the programmer MCP tools or enter the verb editor when you have the appropriate class and progbit.
